<?php

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\LoanBook;
use App\Services\AuditLoggerService;
use App\Services\Maintenance\CommandRunner;
use Illuminate\Http\JsonResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schema;
use Inertia\Inertia;
use Inertia\Response;

/**
 * Maintenance console: run a fixed WHITELIST of artisan commands from the
 * browser, in a background process with live output (ported from the Stress
 * Testing app). The browser only sends a catalogue key and, for a month-end
 * step, a period chosen from the periods the system holds; the command line is
 * built here from a fixed template, so nothing typed reaches the shell.
 * Destructive entries need the confirm phrase typed; one command runs at a
 * time; every launch is written to the audit log.
 */
class MaintenanceController extends Controller
{
    public function __construct(private readonly CommandRunner $runner)
    {
    }

    /**
     * The whitelist. danger: safe | caution | destructive. `period` = the step
     * runs for one month-end ({period}); `{user}` is the signed-in user's id.
     *
     * @return array<int, array<string, mixed>>
     */
    private function catalog(): array
    {
        return [
            // ---------------------------------------------------------------- first-time setup
            ['key' => 'bootstrap', 'group' => 'setup', 'step' => 1,
                'label' => 'Bootstrap the system (first install)',
                'command' => 'eir:bootstrap --fresh --force-wipe --with-client-inputs --build --run-engines --verify --user={user}',
                'description' => 'Wipes this database and rebuilds it from the committed client inputs: seeds roles, governance defaults, staging thresholds and the help centre, lands the E-Banker pack and the take-on workbook, builds every loan book, runs staging, the EIR and the engines, then checks the golden numbers.',
                'danger' => 'destructive', 'confirm' => 'BOOTSTRAP',
                'note' => 'Destroys every record in the connected database. Only for a first install or a deliberate rebuild.'],
            ['key' => 'migrate', 'group' => 'setup', 'step' => 2,
                'label' => 'Apply database updates (migrations)',
                'command' => 'migrate --force',
                'description' => 'Applies any new database migrations shipped with a code update. Existing data is kept.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Take a backup first on a live system (Installation Guide chapter 10).'],
            ['key' => 'seed-permissions', 'group' => 'setup', 'step' => 3,
                'label' => 'Refresh roles and permissions',
                'command' => 'db:seed --class=MaiicAdminPermissionsSeeder --force',
                'description' => 'Adds any permission a new screen needs and grants it to the internal staff roles. Nothing is removed.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Additive.'],
            ['key' => 'seed-governance', 'group' => 'setup', 'step' => 4,
                'label' => 'Add missing governance defaults',
                'command' => 'db:seed --class=GovernanceSettingsSeeder --force',
                'description' => 'Adds the Governance Centre settings a new release introduces, in force from inception. A setting that already exists is never changed.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Additive: approved values are left as they are.'],
            ['key' => 'seed-sicr', 'group' => 'setup', 'step' => 5,
                'label' => 'Seed the qualitative SICR factors',
                'command' => 'db:seed --class=SicrQualitativeFactorsSeeder --force',
                'description' => 'Adds the starter set of qualitative factors (forbearance, borrower condition, agricultural and climate, behavioural, credit-impaired evidence) with the stage each implies.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Additive: existing groups and items are kept.'],

            // ---------------------------------------------------------------- month-end, in order
            ['key' => 'build', 'group' => 'month', 'step' => 1, 'period' => true,
                'label' => 'Build the loan book',
                'command' => 'eir:build-loan-books {period}',
                'description' => 'Builds the month\'s loan book from the landed E-Banker pack by the method in force. A locked month is refused.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Writes the month\'s loan book; approve the build on Imports & Feeds, Loan Book Builds.'],
            ['key' => 'stage', 'group' => 'month', 'step' => 2, 'period' => true,
                'label' => 'Stage the book',
                'command' => 'eir:stage {period} --user={user}',
                'description' => 'Days past due against the governed thresholds, the missed-instalment trigger, then the approved qualitative SICR triggers.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'After re-staging, run the PD and LGD, the forward-looking route and the ECL again.'],
            ['key' => 'segments', 'group' => 'month', 'step' => 3, 'period' => true,
                'label' => 'PD and LGD by segment',
                'command' => 'ifrs9:segment-parameters {period} --user={user}',
                'description' => 'Measures and applies the PD and the LGD of each segment on the governed basis (Governance Centre, PD & LGD segments).',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Clears the month\'s post-FLI PD: run the forward-looking route and the ECL after it.'],
            ['key' => 'fli-correlate', 'group' => 'month', 'step' => 4, 'period' => true,
                'label' => 'Forward-looking: correlation sweep and fits',
                'command' => 'fli:correlate {period}',
                'description' => 'Sweeps the macro series against the credit-loss measures as at the month-end and fits the candidates under the guardrail. Propose and approve a fit on Regression (FLI Adjustments) next.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Writes candidate fits only; nothing reaches a loan until a fit is approved.'],
            ['key' => 'fli-apply', 'group' => 'month', 'step' => 5, 'period' => true,
                'label' => 'Forward-looking: apply the approved fit',
                'command' => 'fli:apply {period} --user={user}',
                'description' => 'Applies the approved fit and the approved scenario set to every loan of the month (the post-FLI PD).',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Refuses when the month has no approved fit or scenario set.'],
            ['key' => 'ecl', 'group' => 'month', 'step' => 6, 'period' => true,
                'label' => 'Calculate the ECL',
                'command' => 'ifrs9:segment-ecl {period} --pd=pd_post_fli',
                'description' => 'The expected credit loss of every portfolio on the post-FLI PD.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Refuses, naming the loans, when a loan with exposure has no stage, PD or LGD.'],
            ['key' => 'revenue', 'group' => 'month', 'step' => 7, 'period' => true,
                'label' => 'EIR revenue',
                'command' => 'eir:run-revenue {period} --user={user}',
                'description' => 'The EIR amortised-cost and interest revenue roll-forward for the month.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Existing rows of the month are left as they are.'],
            ['key' => 'megafarm', 'group' => 'month', 'step' => 8, 'period' => true,
                'label' => 'Mega Farm programme',
                'command' => 'megafarm:ecl {period} --user={user}',
                'description' => 'Runs the Mega Farm programme through the ECL module under its governed scope and method.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Writes the programme\'s ECL run for the month.'],

            // ---------------------------------------------------------------- imports
            ['key' => 'macro', 'group' => 'imports', 'step' => 1,
                'label' => 'Import the World Bank macro series',
                'command' => 'macro:import-worldbank',
                'description' => 'Fetches Malawi\'s macro series from the World Bank with provenance; falls back to the committed snapshot when offline.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'Additive. The scheduler also runs it on the second day of each month.'],
            ['key' => 'feed', 'group' => 'imports', 'step' => 2,
                'label' => 'Land new E-Banker packs from the feed folder',
                'command' => 'eir:poll-feed-folder',
                'description' => 'Lands every new pack found in the feed folder through the gates (route 2). The scheduler runs it every morning at 06:30.',
                'danger' => 'caution', 'note' => 'A pack that fails a gate is quarantined with the file and row named.'],

            // ---------------------------------------------------------------- diagnostics
            ['key' => 'about', 'group' => 'diagnostics', 'step' => 1,
                'label' => 'System snapshot',
                'command' => 'about',
                'description' => 'Application, Laravel and PHP versions, debug mode, caches and drivers. Read only.',
                'danger' => 'safe'],
            ['key' => 'migrate-status', 'group' => 'diagnostics', 'step' => 2,
                'label' => 'Database update status',
                'command' => 'migrate:status',
                'description' => 'Which migrations have run and which are pending. Read only.',
                'danger' => 'safe'],
            ['key' => 'baselines', 'group' => 'diagnostics', 'step' => 3,
                'label' => 'Check the golden numbers',
                'command' => 'eir:baselines',
                'description' => 'Runs the acceptance ties and the golden numbers against the database and reports PASS or FAIL for each.',
                'danger' => 'safe'],
            ['key' => 'smoke-reports', 'group' => 'diagnostics', 'step' => 4,
                'label' => 'Smoke-test the reports',
                'command' => 'ifrs9:smoke-reports',
                'description' => 'Opens every IFRS 9 report and renders its PDF, and reports any that fail.',
                'danger' => 'safe'],
        ];
    }

    public function index(Request $request): Response
    {
        $recent = $this->runner->recent(40);
        $periods = $this->safe(fn () => LoanBook::query()->select('reporting_period')->distinct()
            ->orderByDesc('reporting_period')->limit(36)->pluck('reporting_period')->all(), []);

        return Inertia::render('Admin/Maintenance', [
            'catalog' => array_map(fn ($c) => array_diff_key($c, ['command' => 1]) + ['shown' => $this->shown($c['command'])], $this->catalog()),
            'recent' => $recent,
            'periods' => $periods,
            'status' => [
                'database' => $this->safe(fn () => (string) DB::connection()->getDatabaseName(), null),
                'loan_book_months' => count($periods),
                'latest_month' => $periods[0] ?? null,
                'ecl_months' => $this->safe(fn () => (int) DB::table('reporting_periods')->where('ecl_calculated', 1)->count(), 0),
                'pending_migrations' => null,
                'running' => $this->runner->running(),
            ],
            'can' => ['run' => (bool) $request->user()?->hasRole('admin')],
        ]);
    }

    public function run(Request $request): JsonResponse
    {
        $entry = collect($this->catalog())->firstWhere('key', (string) $request->input('key'));
        if (! $entry) {
            return response()->json(['ok' => false, 'message' => 'Unknown command.'], 422);
        }
        if (($entry['danger'] ?? '') === 'destructive' && (string) $request->input('confirm') !== ($entry['confirm'] ?? '')) {
            return response()->json(['ok' => false, 'message' => 'Type the confirmation phrase to run this command.'], 422);
        }
        if ($busy = $this->runner->running()) {
            return response()->json(['ok' => false, 'message' => "\"{$busy['label']}\" is still running. Wait for it to finish."], 409);
        }

        $period = null;
        if (! empty($entry['period'])) {
            $period = (string) $request->input('period');
            $known = LoanBook::query()->where('reporting_period', $period)->exists();
            if (! preg_match('/^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$/', $period) || (! $known && $entry['key'] !== 'build')) {
                return response()->json(['ok' => false, 'message' => 'Choose a month the system holds a loan book for.'], 422);
            }
            if (! preg_match('/^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$/', $period)) {
                return response()->json(['ok' => false, 'message' => 'Choose a month as YYYY-MM.'], 422);
            }
        }

        $command = strtr($entry['command'], ['{period}' => (string) $period, '{user}' => (string) (int) $request->user()->id]);
        $label = $entry['label'] . ($period ? " ({$period})" : '');
        $id = $this->runner->launch($command, $label, ['danger' => $entry['danger'], 'group' => $entry['group'], 'key' => $entry['key']]);

        AuditLoggerService::log('Maintenance Command Launched', 'maintenance', null, [
            'reporting_period' => $period,
            'new_values' => ['command' => $command, 'danger' => $entry['danger'], 'run_id' => $id],
            'meta' => ['label' => $label],
        ]);

        return response()->json(['ok' => true, 'id' => $id, 'command' => $command]);
    }

    public function output(string $id): JsonResponse
    {
        $status = $this->runner->status($id);

        return $status === null
            ? response()->json(['ok' => false, 'message' => 'Run not found.'], 404)
            : response()->json(['ok' => true, 'run' => $status]);
    }

    /** The command line as the user sees it ({user} stays a placeholder). */
    private function shown(string $command): string
    {
        return 'php artisan ' . str_replace('{user}', '<you>', $command);
    }

    private function safe(callable $fn, mixed $default): mixed
    {
        try {
            return $fn();
        } catch (\Throwable) {
            return $default;
        }
    }
}

                        <h3 class="font-bold text-gray-900">{{ c.label }}</h3>
                    </div>
                    <span class="maiic-badge flex-none" :class="dangerBadge(c.danger)">{{ dangerLabel(c.danger) }}</span>
                </div>
                <p class="mt-2 text-sm text-gray-600">{{ c.description }}</p>
                <code class="mt-3 block truncate rounded bg-gray-50 px-2 py-1 text-[11px] text-gray-600" :title="shownFor(c)">{{ shownFor(c) }}</code>
                <p v-if="c.note" class="mt-2 text-xs text-gray-500">{{ c.note }}</p>
                <div v-if="c.danger === 'destructive'" class="mt-3">
                    <label class="text-[11px] font-bold uppercase tracking-wider text-red-700">Type {{ c.confirm }} to enable</label>
                    <input v-model="typed[c.key]" type="text" class="mt-1 w-full rounded-lg border-red-300 text-sm" :placeholder="c.confirm" autocomplete="off"/>
                </div>
                <div class="mt-auto flex items-center justify-between gap-2 pt-4">
                    <span class="text-[11px] text-gray-400">{{ lastRunText(c) }}</span>
                    <button type="button" @click="start(c)" :disabled="!canStart(c)"
                            class="inline-flex items-center gap-1.5 rounded-lg px-3 py-1.5 text-sm font-bold text-white shadow-sm disabled:cursor-not-allowed disabled:opacity-40"
                            :class="c.danger === 'destructive' ? 'bg-red-600 hover:bg-red-700' : 'bg-maiic-600 hover:bg-maiic-700'">
                        <svg class="h-3.5 w-3.5" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor"><path d="M8 5v14l11-7z"/></svg> Run
                    </button>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>

        <!-- run history -->
        <div v-else class="maiic-panel">
            <table class="maiic-table">
                <thead><tr><th>Started</th><th>Command</th><th>Run by</th><th>Took</th><th>Status</th><th class="num">Output</th></tr></thead>
                <tbody>
                    <tr v-for="r in pagedRecent" :key="r.id">
                        <td class="whitespace-nowrap">{{ fmt(r.started_at) }}</td>
                        <td><div class="font-semibold text-gray-800">{{ r.label }}</div><code class="text-[11px] text-gray-500">{{ r.command }}</code></td>
                        <td>{{ r.started_by || '-' }}</td>
                        <td>{{ r.duration || '-' }}</td>
                        <td><span class="maiic-badge" :class="statusBadge(r.status)">{{ r.status }}</span></td>
                        <td class="num"><button type="button" class="maiic-action maiic-action-view" title="View the output" @click="view(r.id)">
                            <svg class="h-4 w-4" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><path d="M2 12s3.5-7 10-7 10 7 10 7-3.5 7-10 7S2 12 2 12z"/><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="3"/></svg>
                        </button></td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr v-if="!recent.length"><td colspan="6" class="maiic-empty">No command has been run from this console yet.</td></tr>
                </tbody>
            </table>
            <div v-if="recent.length > 15" class="flex items-center gap-1 border-t border-gray-100 px-4 py-3">
                <button v-for="n in Math.ceil(recent.length / 15)" :key="n" type="button" @click="page = n"
                        class="rounded-lg border px-3 py-1 text-sm font-semibold" :class="page === n ? 'border-maiic-600 bg-maiic-600 text-white' : 'border-gray-200 text-gray-700'">{{ n }}</button>
            </div>
        </div>

        <!-- output panel -->
        <div v-if="run" class="fixed inset-y-0 right-0 z-50 flex w-full max-w-2xl flex-col border-l border-gray-200 bg-white shadow-2xl">
            <div class="flex items-start justify-between gap-3 border-b border-gray-100 px-5 py-4">
                <div class="min-w-0">
                    <h3 class="truncate font-bold text-gray-900">{{ run.label }}</h3>
                    <code class="block truncate text-[11px] text-gray-500">{{ run.command }}</code>
                </div>
                <div class="flex flex-none items-center gap-2">
                    <span class="maiic-badge" :class="statusBadge(run.status)">{{ run.status }}{{ run.duration ? ' · ' + run.duration : '' }}</span>
                    <button type="button" class="maiic-action maiic-action-neutral" title="Close" @click="run = null">
                        <svg class="h-4 w-4" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"><path d="M6 6l12 12M18 6L6 18"/></svg>
                    </button>
                </div>
            </div>
            <pre ref="out" class="flex-1 overflow-auto whitespace-pre-wrap bg-gray-950 px-5 py-4 font-mono text-[12px] leading-relaxed text-gray-100">{{ run.output }}</pre>
        </div>
    </app-layout>
</template>

<script>
import AppLayout from '@/Layouts/AppLayout.vue'
import { router } from '@inertiajs/vue3'
import { confirmDialog } from '@/Components/confirmDialog'

const MONTHS = ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun', 'Jul', 'Aug', 'Sep', 'Oct', 'Nov', 'Dec']

export default {
    components: { AppLayout },
    props: { catalog: Array, recent: Array, periods: Array, status: Object, can: Object },
    data() {
        return { tab: 'setup', period: this.nextMonth(this.periods[0]) && this.periods[0], typed: {}, run: null, timer: null, page: 1 }
    },
    computed: {
        tabs() {
            const n = (g) => this.catalog.filter(c => c.group === g).length
            return [
                { key: 'setup', label: 'First-time setup', count: n('setup') },
                { key: 'month', label: 'Month-end', count: n('month') },
                { key: 'imports', label: 'Imports', count: n('imports') },
                { key: 'diagnostics', label: 'Diagnostics', count: n('diagnostics') },
                { key: 'history', label: 'Run history', count: this.recent.length },
            ]
        },
        cards() {
            return this.catalog.filter(c => c.group === this.tab).sort((a, b) => a.step - b.step)
        },
        // the months the system holds, plus the month after the latest (to build it)
        periodChoices() {
            const next = this.nextMonth(this.periods[0])
            return next ? [next, ...this.periods] : this.periods
        },
        pagedRecent() {
            return this.recent.slice((this.page - 1) * 15, this.page * 15)
        },
    },
    methods: {
        nextMonth(p) {
            if (!p) return null
            const [y, m] = p.split('-').map(Number)
            return m === 12 ? `${y + 1}-01` : `${y}-${String(m + 1).padStart(2, '0')}`
        },
        periodLabel(p) {
            if (!p) return '-'
            const [y, m] = String(p).split('-')
            return m ? `${MONTHS[Number(m) - 1]} ${y}` : p
        },
        shownFor(c) {
            return c.period ? c.shown.replace('{period}', this.period || 'YYYY-MM') : c.shown
        },
        fmt(ts) { return ts ? ts.replace('T', ' ').slice(0, 16) : '-' },
        dangerLabel(d) { return { safe: 'Read only', caution: 'Writes data', destructive: 'Destructive' }[d] || d },
        dangerBadge(d) { return { safe: 'maiic-badge-green', caution: 'maiic-badge-gold', destructive: 'maiic-badge-red' }[d] || 'maiic-badge-grey' },
        statusBadge(s) { return { done: 'maiic-badge-green', running: 'maiic-badge-gold', failed: 'maiic-badge-red' }[s] || 'maiic-badge-grey' },
        lastRunText(c) {
            const r = this.recent.find(x => x.label === c.label || x.label.startsWith(c.label + ' ('))
            return r ? `Last: ${this.fmt(r.started_at)} · ${r.status}` : 'Not run from here yet'
        },
        canStart(c) {
            if (!this.can.run || (this.run && this.run.status === 'running')) return false
            if (c.danger === 'destructive') return (this.typed[c.key] || '') === c.confirm
            if (c.period) return !!this.period
            return true
        },
        xsrf() {
            const m = document.cookie.match(/XSRF-TOKEN=([^;]+)/)
            return m ? decodeURIComponent(m[1]) : ''
        },
        async start(c) {
            if (c.danger === 'destructive') {
                if (!(await confirmDialog({ title: 'Wipe and rebuild this database?', message: `${c.label}: every record in ${this.status.database} is destroyed and rebuilt. This cannot be undone.`, confirmLabel: 'Wipe and rebuild', tone: 'danger' }))) return
            } else if (c.danger === 'caution') {
                const when = c.period ? ` for ${this.periodLabel(this.period)}` : ''
                if (!(await confirmDialog({ title: `${c.label}${when}?`, message: c.note || c.description, confirmLabel: 'Run' }))) return
            }
            this.run = { label: c.label, command: this.shownFor(c), status: 'running', output: 'Starting...' }
            try {
                const res = await fetch(route('maintenance.run'), {
                    method: 'POST', credentials: 'same-origin',
                    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Accept: 'application/json', 'X-XSRF-TOKEN': this.xsrf() },
                    body: JSON.stringify({ key: c.key, confirm: this.typed[c.key] || '', period: c.period ? this.period : null }),
                })
                const j = await res.json().catch(() => ({ ok: false, message: res.status === 403 ? 'Refused: running a command is restricted to a system administrator.' : 'The command could not be started.' }))
                if (!j.ok) { this.run = { ...this.run, status: 'failed', output: j.message }; return }
                this.typed[c.key] = ''
                this.poll(j.id)
            } catch (e) {
                this.run = { ...this.run, status: 'failed', output: 'The command could not be started.' }
            }
        },
        poll(id) {
            const tick = async () => {
                try {
                    const j = await (await fetch(route('maintenance.output', id), { credentials: 'same-origin', headers: { Accept: 'application/json' } })).json()
                    if (j.ok) {
                        this.run = { ...j.run, output: j.run.output || '...' }
                        this.$nextTick(() => { if (this.$refs.out) this.$refs.out.scrollTop = this.$refs.out.scrollHeight })
                        if (j.run.status === 'running') { this.timer = setTimeout(tick, 1500); return }
                        router.reload({ only: ['recent', 'status', 'periods'] })
                    }
                } catch (e) { this.timer = setTimeout(tick, 3000) }
            }
            tick()
        },
        async view(id) {
            this.run = { label: '...', command: '', status: 'running', output: 'Loading...' }
            const j = await (await fetch(route('maintenance.output', id), { credentials: 'same-origin', headers: { Accept: 'application/json' } })).json()
            if (j.ok) this.run = { ...j.run, output: j.run.output || '(no output)' }
        },
    },
    beforeUnmount() { if (this.timer) clearTimeout(this.timer) },
}
</script>

# Designing a Complete IFRS 9 Forward-Looking Information (FLI) Module for MAIIC Bank

For a bank such as MAIIC in Malawi, I would design Forward-Looking Information (FLI) as a fully integrated, auditable modelling module within the IFRS 9 system, rather than a page where users simply upload GDP, inflation and other macroeconomic variables and enter an adjustment percentage.

The objective is to allow the bank to perform its IFRS 9 calculations every month, review and update its economic outlook, conduct a comprehensive annual model review, and retain the complete history of what was used to calculate each reporting period's Expected Credit Loss (ECL).

Because your system already calculates Effective Interest Rates (EIR) and discounts expected repayments, FLI must connect directly to the bank's PD, LGD, EAD and expected-cash-flow calculations without incorrectly changing the EIR or double-counting credit losses.

## 1. What IFRS 9 actually requires

IFRS 9 paragraph 5.5.17 requires Expected Credit Loss to reflect three fundamental elements:

1. An unbiased, probability-weighted amount considering possible outcomes.
2. The time value of money.
3. Reasonable and supportable information about historical events, current conditions and future economic forecasts.

Importantly, IFRS 9 does not prescribe a particular statistical model, a fixed number of economic scenarios, or a universal FLI adjustment formula. Those are modelling choices the bank must support, validate and document.&#x20;

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://www.ifrs.org\&sz=32)

IFRS

+2



For MAIIC, I would use this architecture:

Proposed IFRS 9 calculation architecture

Macroeconomic Data & Forecasts

GDP, inflation, policy rates, exchange rates and relevant sector indicators

Baseline

## 50%

Upside

## 20%

Downside

## 30%

Illustrative scenario weights only — bank-approved probabilities required

FLI Transmission Models

Translate macroeconomic forecasts into future portfolio credit risk

PD & Staging

LGD / Recoveries

EAD / Utilisation

Scenario-Level ECL Calculation

Expected contractual cash shortfalls discounted using the applicable IFRS 9 EIR

Probability-Weighted Final ECL

Saved with the reporting period, model versions, scenario assumptions, approvals and audit trail

The most important distinction is that FLI changes expectations about credit risk and cash recoveries, while EIR determines the discounting of the resulting cash shortfalls.

You should therefore build FLI and EIR as connected but separately controlled calculation services.

## 2. How frequently the bank should perform FLI

I would separate annual modelling from monthly ECL processing.

| Activity                  | Frequency                                                    | How it should work                                                 |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Economic data updates     | Monthly or when new data becomes available                   | Import published actuals and revised forecasts                     |
| Scenario review           | Every reporting month                                        | Confirm that existing forecasts and weights remain appropriate     |
| FLI model recalibration   | At least annually, plus event-driven                         | Re-estimate macroeconomic relationships and test model performance |
| FLI scenario approval     | Each new or materially revised scenario set                  | Risk/Finance review with maker-checker approval                    |
| ECL calculation           | Every month-end                                              | Use approved FLI assumptions applicable to that date               |
| EIR calculation           | Origination, with required subsequent accounting adjustments | Preserve original EIR and applicable rate history                  |
| EIR-based ECL discounting | Every ECL run                                                | Discount future cash shortfalls to reporting date                  |
| Backtesting               | Monthly monitoring, deeper annual validation                 | Compare earlier forecasts with actual outcomes                     |

One crucial point: the bank should not automatically reuse January's forecasts for December without evaluating whether they remain reasonable at December's reporting date.

Monthly ECL calculations should always reference an approved, reporting-date-appropriate economic outlook, even if the bank decides that an existing forecast set remains suitable.

## 3. How I would design the FLI module user interface

I would introduce a separate top-level Forward-Looking Information menu in the IFRS 9 system.

Rather than putting everything on one very long page, I would use a dashboard, a guided scenario workbench and a set of dedicated modelling screens.

### Proposed navigation

MAIIC | IFRS 9

Illustrative UI

&#x20;Dashboard

&#x20;Data Management

&#x20;PD, LGD & EAD

&#x20;Forward-Looking Information

Overview

Economic Indicators

Scenario Workbench

Model Calibration

FLI Impact Analysis

Approval & History

&#x20;EIR & Cash Flows

&#x20;ECL Results

FLI OVERVIEW

## October 2026

Economic indicators

# 6

Illustrative configured variables

Economic scenarios

# 3

Base, upside and downside

Current forecast vintage

2026-10 v1

Approval and publication tracked

Month-end controls

Data completeness → Model validation → Scenario approval → ECL run

The individual screens should work as follows.

### Screen A — Economic Indicators

This is where bank users manage macroeconomic information from sources such as the Reserve Bank of Malawi, National Statistical Office, IMF and World Bank.

It should support importing both historical actuals and future forecasts, but maintain a clear distinction between them.

Example data table (all values below are illustrative, not actual Malawi forecasts):

| Indicator            | 2024 Actual | 2025 Actual | 2026 Forecast | 2027 Forecast |
| -------------------- | ----------- | ----------- | ------------- | ------------- |
| Real GDP growth      | 2.0%        | 2.5%        | 3.2%          | 4.1%          |
| Inflation            | 27.0%       | 23.0%       | 20.0%         | 16.0%         |
| Policy rate          | 26.0%       | 25.0%       | 23.0%         | 21.0%         |
| Exchange rate change | 18.0%       | 14.0%       | 12.0%         | 9.0%          |

Every observation should include its source, release date, reporting period, unit, observation type (actual, estimate or forecast), and the date it became available to the bank.

That last requirement is important for historical reproducibility. A forecast published in October 2026 must not silently replace the forecast that was actually available when the bank closed its accounts in March 2026.

The UI should offer Excel/CSV import, manual entry, validation, historical charts, source-document attachments and revision comparisons.

### Screen B — Scenario Workbench

This is where the bank constructs future economic conditions.

Here is an interactive example of how I would organize that screen. The percentages and FLI impacts are simulated to demonstrate the design, not MAIIC model outputs.

## Scenario Workbench

Economic assumptions and scenario probabilities

Draft simulation

Reporting periodOctober 2026

Forecast horizon

2026–2028

Scenario probabilities

Upside

20%

Baseline

50%

Downside

30%

Total probability

## 100%

Economic scenario forecasts

UpsideBaseDownside

| Indicator  | 2026  | 2027  | 2028  |
| ---------- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| GDP growth | 3.2%  | 4.1%  | 4.5%  |
| Inflation  | 20.0% | 16.0% | 13.0% |

This interactive prototype is for exploring the interface. It does not save changes to a bank database or calculate a validated FLI model.

In the actual system, I would also include monthly forecasts, charts comparing scenario trajectories, an economic rationale field, forecast-source attachments and model-generated scenarios that can be reviewed before approval.

Users must be able to save drafts without affecting previous approved forecasts.

### Screen C — Model Calibration

This is arguably the most important screen.

Many IFRS 9 implementations do not model the statistical relationship between economic conditions and credit defaults adequately. Instead, they apply an arbitrary PD uplift.

The screen should allow the bank to examine how macroeconomic variables affect credit risk, for example by estimating:

\\[ \operatorname{logit}(PD\_{s,t}) = \beta_0+\beta_1 GDP\_{s,t} +\beta_2 Inflation\_{s,t} +\beta_3 Rate\_{s,t} \\]

Here \\(s\\) represents the scenario and \\(t\\) the forecast period.

This is an example of a possible model specification, not a prescribed IFRS 9 formula. The bank could instead use a transition-matrix model, survival model, satellite model, calibrated multipliers or another validated method.

I would design the calibration page around three panels:

- Data selection: choose portfolio, historical default observations, macroeconomic variables, date range and lags.
- Model evaluation: coefficients, confidence intervals, predictive accuracy, economic plausibility, stability, backtesting results and diagnostic tests.
- Model publication: version, effective date, validation documents, approval and whether it is authorized for production ECL.

For example:

| Model      | Portfolio     | Proposed macro drivers                 | Status       |
| ---------- | ------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| PD-FLI-01  | Retail loans  | GDP, inflation                         | Example only |
| PD-FLI-02  | SME loans     | GDP, rates, FX                         | Example only |
| LGD-FLI-01 | Secured loans | Collateral prices, recovery conditions | Example only |

The choice of macroeconomic variables must be justified by historical evidence, economic reasoning and the portfolio's risk characteristics.

Importantly, the system should support segment-specific model configurations rather than assuming the same GDP sensitivity across every loan type.

### Screen D — FLI Impact Analysis

Before approving new assumptions, users should compare the current proposed FLI output with the previously approved assumptions.

FLI Impact Analysis

Simulated values

ECL before FLI

# MWK 10.00bn

Weighted ECL after FLI

# MWK 11.95bn

+19.5%

0bn5bn10bn15bn20bnUpsideBaseDownside

Illustrative ECL amounts in MWK billions; not actual bank results.

| Upside (20%)         | MWK 8.00bn  |
| -------------------- | ----------- |
| Base (50%)           | MWK 11.00bn |
| Downside (30%)       | MWK 16.00bn |
| Probability-weighted | MWK 11.90bn |

Scenario-weighted result: (8 × 20%) + (11 × 50%) + (16 × 30%) = MWK 11.90bn. The simulated summary above should therefore display MWK 11.90bn and +19.0%; the independently illustrative summary figures are not the reconciliation result.

In the production dashboard, all headline metrics must come directly from the same calculated results table to avoid any discrepancy between KPIs, charts and detailed workings.

The impact screen should also explain changes by portfolio, stage, scenario, macroeconomic driver, model version and manual adjustment. Users should be able to drill down to individual facilities.

## 4. Database design — the tables I would create

For a Laravel and MySQL-based IFRS 9 platform, I would organize the database into five groups. These are logical tables rather than an exhaustive physical schema.

### A. Macroeconomic data tables

| Table                  | Important columns                                                           | Purpose                                     |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `macro_variables`      | id, code, name, unit, frequency, country, active                            | Master list of economic variables           |
| `macro_observations`   | variable_id, period, value, value_type, source_id, release_date, vintage_id | Historical actuals, estimates and forecasts |
| `macro_sources`        | id, institution, publication, reference_url                                 | Stores the origin of economic information   |
| `macro_import_batches` | id, filename, checksum, imported_by, status, errors                         | Tracks imports and data-quality checks      |
| `macro_vintages`       | id, as_of_date, published_at, source_version                                | Preserves historical forecast releases      |

The observations table might contain:

| Variable  | Period | Value | Type     | Forecast vintage |
| --------- | ------ | ----- | -------- | ---------------- |
| GDP       | 2025   | 2.5%  | Actual   | 2026-10          |
| GDP       | 2026   | 3.2%  | Forecast | 2026-10          |
| GDP       | 2027   | 4.1%  | Forecast | 2026-10          |
| Inflation | 2026   | 20.0% | Forecast | 2026-10          |

All figures here are examples.

The critical design rule is that one variable can have multiple observations for the same period from different published vintages, but an ECL run must reference exactly which value and vintage it used.

### B. Scenario tables

| Table                  | Important columns                                  | Purpose                                           |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `fli_scenario_sets`    | id, reporting_date, vintage_id, version, status    | A complete set of scenarios for a reporting date  |
| `fli_scenarios`        | id, scenario_set_id, name, probability, narrative  | Base, upside, downside or other scenarios         |
| `fli_scenario_values`  | scenario_id, variable_id, forecast_period, value   | Monthly/annual economic forecasts                 |
| `fli_scenario_weights` | scenario_id, segment_id, weight, valid_from        | Optional segment-specific weights where justified |
| `fli_scenario_reviews` | set_id, reviewer, decision, rationale, reviewed_at | Governance and scenario review                    |

I would treat the scenario set as the versioned container of all assumptions used in a particular month-end.

Once published, a scenario set should be immutable. Revisions create a new version rather than modifying an old approved record.

### C. FLI model tables

| Table                    | Important columns                                                    | Purpose                                   |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `fli_models`             | id, target_metric, segment_id, methodology                           | Defines PD, LGD or EAD transmission model |
| `fli_model_versions`     | id, model_id, version, calibration_date, status                      | Version-controlled specifications         |
| `fli_model_coefficients` | model_version_id, variable_id, lag, coefficient                      | Estimated macroeconomic sensitivities     |
| `fli_model_diagnostics`  | model_version_id, metric, value, result                              | Validation and backtesting results        |
| `fli_model_assignments`  | segment_id, target_metric, model_version_id                          | Maps model to portfolio                   |
| `fli_overlays`           | id, scenario_set_id, segment_id, rationale, amount_or_factor, status | Separately approved expert overlays       |

Additional tables should preserve calibration samples, data transformations, forecast methodologies, coefficient uncertainty and independent validation results.

### D. Scenario-specific credit risk calculations

| Table                    | Important columns                                                           | Purpose                             |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `fli_projection_runs`    | id, scenario_set_id, run_date, status                                       | A complete FLI projection run       |
| `fli_pd_term_structures` | run_id, segment_id, scenario_id, period, marginal_pd, survival_probability  | Future probabilities of default     |
| `fli_lgd_projections`    | run_id, scenario_id, segment_id, period, lgd                                | Scenario-adjusted recovery severity |
| `fli_ead_projections`    | run_id, scenario_id, facility_id, period, ead                               | Projected outstanding exposure      |
| `fli_sicr_assessments`   | run_id, facility_id, origination_risk, current_lifetime_risk, stage, reason | Forward-looking staging assessment  |
| `fli_ecl_results`        | ecl_run_id, facility_id, scenario_id, stage, ecl_amount                     | Scenario-level ECL                  |
| `fli_weighted_ecl`       | ecl_run_id, facility_id, weighted_ecl                                       | Final probability-weighted ECL      |

For very large loan books, do not store all facility-level term structures in one unpartitioned table. Use reporting-date partitioning, appropriate compound indexes and separate aggregate results from detailed calculation evidence.

### E. EIR and cash-flow integration tables

These are especially relevant because your platform already handles effective interest calculations and discounted repayment profiles.

| Table                         | Important columns                                                                         | Purpose                                                     |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `eir_calculations`            | facility_id, original_eir, rate_basis, calculation_version, status                        | Initial EIR calculation and lineage                         |
| `eir_rate_history`            | facility_id, effective_date, applicable_eir, reason                                       | Relevant variable-rate or modification-related rate history |
| `contractual_cashflows`       | facility_id, due_date, principal, interest, eligible_fees                                 | Contractual payment schedule                                |
| `expected_cashflow_scenarios` | facility_id, scenario_id, payment_date, expected_receipt, recovery_type                   | Scenario-specific expected receipts                         |
| `discounted_cashflows`        | ecl_run_id, facility_id, scenario_id, date, discount_rate, discount_factor, present_value | Discounted cash-flow evidence                               |
| `ecl_run_snapshots`           | ecl_run_id, loanbook_id, fli_set_id, pd_version, lgd_version, eir_version                 | Complete reproducibility record                             |

For performance, detailed scenario cash flows can also be stored in partitioned calculation-result tables, provided the bank retains auditable calculations.

A useful database design principle is that every ECL result has a traceable path to the source loan, approved scenario set, model versions, projected cash flows and EIR used.

## 5. End-to-end workflow for monthly IFRS 9 reporting

I would create a single guided workflow, rather than requiring bank users to visit seven unrelated pages and remember which tasks must be completed.

1. Create month-end reporting period

   Select October 2026, establish cutoff date and lock the reporting context.
2. Load and validate source data

   Import the loan book, repayment transactions, contractual cash flows, write-offs, recoveries and available macroeconomic updates.
3. Review economic assumptions

   Check actual economic data, forecast revisions, scenario weights, relevant stress events and existing model suitability.
4. Run FLI projections

   Calculate scenario-sensitive PD, LGD, EAD and lifetime credit risk. Run quality controls and model coverage checks.
5. Calculate staging, EIR and ECL

   Assess SICR, apply the appropriate stage, calculate credit shortfalls and discount them using the applicable EIR.
6. Review results and reconcile

   Compare ECL movements against the prior month, including portfolio, stage, balance, model, scenario and overlay impacts.
7. Approve and close

   Risk and Finance approve the results, the reporting snapshot is frozen, and audit workbooks and reports become available.

The user should see the readiness of each step, with a clear explanation of any failure.

For example, if October's loan book is available but the model has no approved October-applicable FLI assumptions, the system should not silently default to historical PDs and produce a final official result.

It should show an explicit exception requiring approval of suitable assumptions.

## 6. Annual FLI review: what happens differently?

The annual FLI process should have a dedicated Model Review & Recalibration workflow, separate from the monthly scenario review.

During the annual cycle, the bank should be able to upload new years of historical default data, evaluate additional macroeconomic variables, rebuild modelling datasets, recalibrate candidate models and compare them against the current approved models.

The annual workbench should include out-of-time validation, observed-versus-predicted default rates, scenario sensitivity, parameter stability, portfolio segmentation and model limitations.

A new model should follow a controlled lifecycle:

`Draft → Calibration → Validation → Risk Review → Approval → Published`

The bank should be able to compare the revised model with the previous version using the same loan-book snapshot before publishing it.

Annual recalibration is not a reason to rewrite old figures. The December 2025 approved reporting results must remain reproducible even after a new model is introduced for 2026.

## 7. How FLI should interact with PD, LGD, EAD, EIR and repayments

This is the area where I would be particularly careful with the MAIIC implementation.

### A. FLI and probability of default

Suppose a retail portfolio has a historically calibrated 12-month PD of 5%.

Once macroeconomic forecasts are applied, its conditional probabilities might change:

| Scenario | Conditional 12-month PD |
| -------- | ----------------------- |
| Upside   | 3.5%                    |
| Base     | 5.0%                    |
| Downside | 8.0%                    |

Using illustrative weights of 20%, 50% and 30%, the weighted PD would be:

\\[ PD\_{\mathrm{weighted}} =0.20(3.5\\%)+0.50(5\\%)+0.30(8\\%) =\boxed{5.6\\%} \\]

However, this is a simplified one-period calculation.

For actual Stage 2 lifetime ECL, I would not multiply the initial 12-month PD by the remaining number of years or blindly apply one uplift to a lifetime PD.

The engine should generate a scenario-specific marginal PD term structure, including survival probability and defaults in each future period.

### B. FLI and LGD

For secured facilities, economic forecasts can influence expected recovery values, recovery costs and the timing of collateral realization.

The LGD model might generate:

| Scenario | Illustrative LGD |
| -------- | ---------------- |
| Upside   | 30%              |
| Base     | 35%              |
| Downside | 45%              |

If the existing LGD calculation already embeds adverse collateral assumptions, applying another downside adjustment to the same risk can double-count losses.

The bank should clearly identify which risk drivers are already included in historical LGD and which are introduced through FLI.

### C. FLI and EAD

EAD generally follows expected outstanding exposures, scheduled amortization and, where relevant, future drawings and credit conversion factors.

For a fully drawn amortizing term loan, the expected balance may decline each month according to the repayment profile.

For an overdraft or revolving exposure, stressed economic conditions might affect drawings, utilization and future exposures.

The FLI engine therefore needs to connect to the facility-level repayment schedule rather than assume that every loan maintains its current outstanding balance until maturity.

### D. FLI and EIR

Here is the distinction I would preserve in the architecture.

| Item                   | What it represents                                 | How FLI affects it                                                 |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| EIR                    | Effective financing yield determined under IFRS 9  | FLI does not ordinarily change original fixed-rate EIR             |
| Contractual cash flows | Payments due under the loan contract               | Not directly rewritten merely because the economic outlook changes |
| Expected cash flows    | Amounts and timing expected to be received         | Can change under different economic scenarios                      |
| Discount factor        | Converts future cash flows to reporting-date value | Uses the appropriate IFRS 9 discount rate                          |
| ECL                    | Present value of expected credit shortfalls        | Changes with scenario-specific default and recovery expectations   |

Under IFRS 9, ECL is generally discounted using the EIR determined at initial recognition or an appropriate approximation. Floating-rate instruments and purchased or originated credit-impaired assets have particular rules that must be handled separately.&#x20;

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://www.ifrs.org\&sz=32)

IFRS

+1



Do not apply the current Malawi policy rate as the ECL discount rate simply because it is part of the FLI forecast.

The policy rate may explain how credit risk evolves. It does not replace the facility's IFRS 9 EIR.

### E. How FLI and discounted repayments should work together

Consider a simplified example.

A loan has a 12% annual effective interest rate, a contractual payment of MWK 110,000 in one year, and the following possible expected payments:

| Scenario | Expected receipt | Cash shortfall |
| -------- | ---------------- | -------------- |
| Upside   | MWK 108,000      | MWK 2,000      |
| Base     | MWK 100,000      | MWK 10,000     |
| Downside | MWK 80,000       | MWK 30,000     |

For this simple annual example:

\\[ PV(\text{shortfall}\_s) =\frac{\text{Contractual CF}-\text{Expected CF}\_s}{1+EIR} \\]

The discounted ECL per scenario becomes approximately:

| Scenario | Discounted ECL |
| -------- | -------------- |
| Upside   | MWK 1,786      |
| Base     | MWK 8,929      |
| Downside | MWK 26,786     |

With the same 20%, 50% and 30% weights:

\\[ ECL\_{\mathrm{weighted}} =0.20(1,786)+0.50(8,929)+0.30(26,786) \\]

\\[ \boxed{ECL\approx MWK\ 12,857} \\]

This illustrates the correct relationship: the economic scenarios influence the expected receipts, while the applicable EIR discounts the resulting shortfalls.

For real loan portfolios, calculations require individual payment dates, actual day counts, expected recovery dates, default timing, staging and the bank's approved cash-flow methodology.

### F. Stage 1, Stage 2 and Stage 3 treatment

I would implement the stage-specific treatment as follows:

| Stage   | FLI application                           | Calculation basis                                                                        |
| ------- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Stage 1 | Forward-looking 12-month default risk     | Lifetime cash shortfalls arising from defaults possible in the next 12 months            |
| Stage 2 | Forward-looking lifetime default risk     | Cash shortfalls arising from defaults possible over expected life                        |
| Stage 3 | Forward-looking cash recovery assumptions | Probability-weighted discounted expected credit shortfalls for credit-impaired exposures |

For Stage 1, remember that a 12-month ECL is not necessarily the cash shortfall occurring within the next 12 months. It includes lifetime shortfalls associated with defaults that could occur during that 12-month default window.

For Stage 2, a simplified discrete-time approach is:

\\[ ECL_s = \sum\_{t=1}^{T} mPD\_{s,t}\times LGD\_{s,t}\times EAD\_{s,t}\times DF_t \\]

Where \\(mPD\\) is the marginal probability of default for period \\(t\\), accounting for survival to that period.

The final provision is:

\\[ ECL\_{\mathrm{final}}=\sum\_{s=1}^{S}w_sECL_s \\]

This PD/LGD/EAD expression is an approximation requiring consistency with the contractual cash-shortfall definition and recovery timing.

For Stage 3, especially where MAIIC already calculates discounted repayments and recoveries, I would make the cash-flow shortfall approach the primary valuation method whenever reliable facility-level projections exist:

\\[ ECL_s = PV(\text{Contractual CF}) - PV(\text{Expected CF}\_s) \\]

The precise implementation must reconcile to the asset's gross carrying amount under IFRS 9. It should not automatically multiply an already credit-impaired facility's discounted shortfall by a separate PD that would recognize the same default risk again.

Also, if a Stage 3 expected cash-flow model already reflects recoveries from security, the system must not deduct the same collateral benefit a second time.

This is why I would build one shared cash-flow and discounting service used by all stages, with the appropriate stage-specific ECL methodology.

## 8. Controls and reconciliation I would make compulsory

An IFRS 9 FLI module should have proper audit controls from the beginning, not added after an audit identifies issues.

These are the most important automated checks:

| Control                                                  | Expected action                                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Scenario probabilities do not total 100%                 | Block scenario publication                                     |
| Forecast is missing for a required period                | Flag missing information and block an unsupported official run |
| Unapproved model version selected                        | Block official ECL                                             |
| Loan has no valid EIR or applicable discount rate        | Flag for controlled resolution, not silent zero                |
| Facility has no portfolio model assignment               | Report unmapped exposure                                       |
| Scenario PD outside valid probability bounds             | Block invalid results                                          |
| Inconsistent monthly/annual macro units                  | Block until corrected                                          |
| Scenario already includes a risk also applied as overlay | Require double-counting review                                 |
| ECL differs significantly from prior period              | Require investigation and commentary                           |
| Approved forecast subsequently revised                   | Retain old version and create a new one                        |

The bank should also have an ECL movement reconciliation showing opening ECL, balance movements, new facilities, derecognition, stage transfers, changes in credit risk, FLI movements, recoveries and other relevant adjustments.

For the illustrative FLI dashboard above, the reconciled scenario-weighted ECL is MWK 11.90 billion, representing a 19.0% increase over MWK 10.00 billion before FLI. Those are the values the headline KPIs should display.

## 9. Reports and Excel audit workbooks

I would make the following exports available from the FLI module:

- Macroeconomic Data Workbook: historical actuals, forecasts, source references and revisions.
- Scenario Workbook: upside, baseline and downside paths, weights and rationale.
- Model Calibration Workbook: datasets, coefficients, model diagnostics and validation results.
- PD/LGD/EAD FLI Workbook: scenario-specific projected risk parameters and term structures.
- EIR & Discounted Cash-Flow Workbook: contractual payments, expected receipts, discount factors and present values.
- FLI Impact & ECL Reconciliation Workbook: weighted ECL, movements, stage changes and driver attribution.
- Approval & Audit Workbook: users, timestamps, model versions, scenario versions and signed-off decisions.

Each export should include a report-date identifier and run ID so that someone reviewing the 31 October 2026 report can reproduce its workings without using revised November assumptions.

## 10. How I would implement this in your Laravel IFRS 9 system

I would separate the calculation engine into services with explicit inputs and outputs.

| Service                     | Responsibility                                                    |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `MacroDataService`          | Validates macroeconomic observations and vintages                 |
| `ScenarioSetService`        | Manages forecasts, scenario weights and approvals                 |
| `FliCalibrationService`     | Calibrates and validates credit risk relationships                |
| `FliProjectionService`      | Generates scenario-specific PD, LGD and EAD                       |
| `SicrAssessmentService`     | Determines forward-looking credit deterioration and staging       |
| `EirCalculationService`     | Determines and maintains applicable EIR                           |
| `CashflowProjectionService` | Constructs contractual and scenario-dependent expected cash flows |
| `DiscountingService`        | Calculates present values using IFRS 9 discount conventions       |
| `EclCalculationService`     | Calculates scenario ECL and probability-weighted provision        |
| `EclReconciliationService`  | Attributes changes in ECL and produces audit evidence             |

The complete process should look like this:

Loan Book + Repayment Schedules + Macro Data

EIR Engine

Rates, amortized cost, discount conventions

FLI Engine

Forecasts, scenarios, PD, LGD, EAD

Staging + Expected Cash-Flow Engine

Time-dependent defaults, scheduled receipts and recoveries

Scenario-Specific Discounted ECL

Weighted Final ECL + Audit Evidence

Month-end results, reconciliation, approval and reporting

## 11. What I would prioritize for MAIIC

Given that the system already has an EIR engine and discounted repayment calculations, I would not rebuild those parts merely to add FLI.

I would implement the following in order:

1. Build the macroeconomic data and scenario management module, including source data, historical forecast vintages, probability weights and approvals.
2. Build the model calibration and projection engine, initially focusing on PD and adding scenario-sensitive LGD/EAD where material and supportable.
3. Integrate the projections into staging and the existing cash-flow engine, ensuring EIR discounting is preserved and credit losses are not counted twice.
4. Introduce a monthly FLI review and close workflow, so users can update forecasts, compare ECL impacts and authorize a reporting run.
5. Add independent validation, backtesting, reconciliation and audit exports, including full traceability from macroeconomic forecasts to facility-level ECL.

The key design decision is that the FLI module should not merely produce an adjusted PD percentage. It should produce a versioned, approved, scenario-specific credit risk projection that the ECL engine can consume for the appropriate reporting date.

That will allow MAIIC to perform monthly ECL calculations while maintaining a controlled annual modelling process, and it will make the connection between forward-looking assumptions, EIR, discounted repayments and final provisions transparent to auditors.

The methodology should ultimately be aligned to MAIIC's approved accounting policy, validated using its loan and default history, and reviewed against IFRS 9 and applicable Malawi regulatory requirements. The EBA's guidance is also a useful reference for model governance, validation and the treatment of forward-looking economic information, although it is not itself Malawi regulation.&#x20;

--- content ---
---
kicker: MAIIC | IFRS 9 FORWARD-LOOKING INFORMATION
title: The forward-looking module, specification version 1
subtitle: How the economy enters MAIIC's expected credit loss: what is built, what is missing, the target design, the decisions, and the order of work
date: 13 October 2026
prepared: Prepared by Dupleix Institute for the Malawi Agricultural and Industrial Investment Corporation plc (MAIIC)
people: Project sponsor Dr Thomson Kumwenda, CFO | Engagement lead Edward Mazibuko CA(SA) | Build lead Kundai Muriwo
status: Draft for review. Builds on specification version 4, sections 13 (macro statistics), 14 (forward-looking adjustments) and 15 (economic scenarios), which stay in force; where this document decides something new, it says so and it governs for the forward-looking module.

## 0. Why this document, and how to read it

A proposal for a complete forward-looking information (FLI) module was put to the team on 13 October 2026. It describes the module a bank should have: macroeconomic data with its history of forecasts, governed scenarios, calibrated models, scenario-level ECL, discounting at the effective interest rate, a monthly close and an annual review, controls and audit workbooks.

The proposal is right in its principles. Most of what it asks for already exists in the MAIIC system, some of it under other names, and some of it is missing. This document does three things: it maps the proposal onto what is built (section 2), it records the decisions that close the gaps (section 3), and it sets the target design and the order of work (sections 4 to 9). Section 10 lists what MAIIC and Dr Thom are asked to decide.

One rule runs through all of it: **the module extends what exists; it does not build a second forward-looking process beside the first.** A parallel set of tables is how the legacy tools came about (now kept under Administration, Legacy FLI tools, and not used by the ECL).

## 1. What IFRS 9 asks for

| Requirement | Where | What it means for MAIIC |
|---|---|---|
| An unbiased, probability-weighted amount, from a range of possible outcomes | 5.5.17(a), B5.5.42 | More than one scenario where the loss responds non-linearly to the economy; the loss is weighted, not the economy |
| The time value of money | 5.5.17(b), B5.5.44 | Shortfalls discounted at the effective interest rate set at initial recognition; for a floating-rate asset, the current effective rate |
| Reasonable and supportable information about past events, current conditions and forecasts, without undue cost | 5.5.17(c), B5.5.49 to B5.5.54 | Only information available at the reporting date; forecasts may lean on long-run averages beyond the reasonable forecast horizon |
| 12-month ECL in Stage 1, lifetime in Stage 2 and 3 | 5.5.3, 5.5.5 | The forward-looking view enters the PD over the right window: one year for Stage 1, the remaining life for Stage 2 |
| Credit-impaired assets | Appendix A, B5.5.33 | Stage 3 is measured on the shortfall of expected cash flows; no further PD is applied on top of the default that has happened |

IFRS 9 does not prescribe a model, a number of scenarios, or a formula for the adjustment. Each is a choice MAIIC makes, supports with evidence, documents and keeps under review.

## 2. The proposal against what is built

| The proposal asks for | In the MAIIC system today | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Macroeconomic variables, observations, sources and import batches | Macro Statistics (`macro_statistics`, `macro_statistics_data`, `macro_source_import_batches`), World Bank fetch with an offline snapshot, IMF WEO and RBM policy-rate files, the bridge to monthly series (`macro_series`) | Built (spec v4 section 13) |
| Forecast vintages: a value as known on a date | Every FLI read goes through `AsAtSeries` (commit ac12c36): a period sees only what was knowable by its end, with a governed publication lag per series | Built in the engine; **gap:** the vintage is the load date, not the publisher's release date |
| Scenario sets, versioned, approved, immutable once published | `governed_scenario_sets`, `governed_scenarios`, `scenario_shocks`; proposed by one person, approved by another, locked with the period; rules (at least 3 scenarios, base at least 40 percent, no weight above 60 percent, a calibration note on every downside); back-test and sensitivity | Built (spec v4 section 15) |
